01 / THE CHALLENGE

A portfolio that could become a studio

I created Add Art's website to establish a distinctive online portfolio and build the foundation for a digital-first design studio. The challenge was to represent both my creative identity and the strategic value of my work, while making services and projects easy to discover.

02 / MY ROLE & PROCESS

Designer, client and developer

I was also my own client. I identified the studio's needs and developed the website alongside my UX/UI Development training, progressively refining the information structure, visual language and front-end. I worked across brand direction, interface design, content composition and implementation with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

03 / UX & INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE

Making a multidisciplinary offer navigable

A key challenge was separating services into dedicated pages without losing coherence across the experience. The source includes pages for UX research, prototyping, websites, visual identity and editorial design, alongside individual project pages, contact and briefing flows. This structure gives visitors distinct entry points into the studio's offer.

04 / VISUAL DESIGN

A recognisable editorial identity

The visual direction balances an editorial aesthetic with practical navigation. Typography, colour and composition were chosen to express the studio's identity rather than rely on generic templates. Responsive behaviour and search discoverability were priorities during development. The code includes page-specific titles and descriptions, responsive CSS and reduced-motion rules.

05 / FROM DESIGN TO BROWSER

Implementation, interaction and AI-assisted workflows

I built the site using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using Claude, ChatGPT and other AI tools to support debugging, CSS organisation and experimentation. I directed and edited the visual compositions and video assets. The source includes an interactive portfolio gallery, a briefing flow using EmailJS, and JavaScript interactions. I treated AI-generated suggestions as material to evaluate and refine, not as a substitute for design decisions.

06 / THE HARDEST PART

Connecting content, interaction and delivery

The most demanding work was structuring separate service pages, configuring email delivery from the briefing experience and developing the gallery-like portfolio interaction. These challenges made the relationship between interface design, code and user flows tangible: an experience is only complete when its interactions work beyond the mockup.

07 / OUTCOME

A functioning foundation, not a finished endpoint

The result is a multi-page studio website with service descriptions, project case pages, portfolio browsing and a project briefing interface. The supplied version 3.4 contains 19 HTML pages, a shared CSS stylesheet and JavaScript. This is evidence of implementation scope; no conversion, traffic, performance or usability metrics are claimed.

08 / WHAT I WOULD IMPROVE

A clearer system for the next iteration

My immediate priorities are to keep the skills and portfolio content up to date and add stronger project evidence. From a technical perspective, I would also review CSS maintainability and reusable patterns, then validate the experience with structured accessibility, mobile and performance testing. These are proposed next steps, not claims that the current site fails those tests.
